newsitem.title: USA: Detroit Diesel to buy Outboard Marine.
newsitem.headline: Detroit Diesel to buy Outboard Marine.

text.p: Detroit Diesel Corp. said Wednesday it reached a definitive agreement to acquire Outboard Marine Corp. in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $500 million, including debt.

Detroit Diesel said it will launch a $16 per share cash tender offer for about 67 percent of the outstanding shares of Waukegan, Ill.-based Outboard Marine, which makes Johnson and Evinrude outboard engines and Chris-Craft and Grumman boats.
The company will then purchase the remaining Outboard Marine shares for a combination of cash and 4 million shares of Detroit Diesel common stock, the company said.
Detroit Diesel is a wholly owned unit of Penske Corp., a closely held group of transport-related companies headed by auto racing entrepreneur Roger Penske.
"The aggregate value of the transaction is approximately $500 million, including the assumption of OMC's existing debt of approximately $180 million," Detroit Diesel said.
In addition to the equity offering, the acquisition will be financed through a new credit facility, the company said.

The agreement, subject to customary conditions, provides for merger of a new Detroit Diesel unit with Outboard Marine, the largest U.S. manufacturer of outboard marine engines and the second-largest maker of recreational powerboats.
The board of directors of Outboard Marine approved the offer and the merger, Detroit Diesel said.
"Our objective is to further expand our worldwide marine capabilities beyond diesel engines with the OMC enterprises," said Penske, who is chairman of Detroit Diesel.
Detroit Diesel makes heavy-duty diesel and other engines for trucks, buses, power generation, cars, boats, military vehicles and construction, mining and industrial equipment.
The Penske group has annual revenues exceeding $6 billion, Detroit Diesel said.
Outboard Marine's stock closed Tuesday at $19.4375 on the New York Stock Exchange. Detroit Diesel ended at $23.75, also on the NYSE.
